LD 562 -- An Act to Update Reimbursement Rates for Transportation of Deceased Persons by Funeral Homes When the Transport is at the Request of the Chief Medical Examiner
Position: Support
Testimony By:
Adam Walker, President - Maine Funeral Directors Association
March 25, 2025
Senator lngwersen, Rep. Meyer and Members ofthe Health and Human Services Committee. My name is Adam Walker, and writing to you today as President of the Maine
Funeral Directors Association in support of LD 562, An Act to Update Reimbursement
Rates for Transportation of Deceased Persons by Funeral Homes When the Transport is at
the Request of the Chief Medical Examiner."
Funeral service practitioners across the state play a crucial role in assisting the Office of
the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) in transporting deceased persons with dignity and professionalism. However, the reimbursement rates currently in place do not reflect the
true costs of providing this essential service.
Background and Need for LD 562
~ The last increase in transportation reimbursement rates occurred in 201 1. Before that, the rates had not been adjusted since 1998.
- Since the last increase, the costs of labor, fuel, vehicle maintenance, licensing fees, and insurance have risen significantly. The price of a removalvehicle alone has increased from $24,000 in 2011 to over $30,000 today.
- Many funeral homes are currently providing this service at a financial loss, which
threatens the ability of practitioners to continue offering this critical support to the OCME
and Maine families.
Why This Matters
1. Ensuring Funeral Homes Can Sustain This Service
- Many funeral homes operate on thin margins, and absorbing transportation costs at a loss is unsustainable. Without appropriate reimbursement, some practitioners may no

longer be able to provide this service, which would create challenges for the OCME and
delay crucial forensic investigations.

2. Supporting Families in Difficult Times

- Funeral practitioners are often the first professionals' families interact with after a loss.
They provide compassion, dignity, and reassurance while navigating complex and
emotional situations. Without this support, Maine families may face additional stress and
logistical burdens.
3. Maintaining Public Safety and OCME Operations
- If funeral homes can no longer afford to provide transportation, the burden will fall on
local governments or law enforcement agencies, leading to increased costs and logistical
challenges.

- Timely transportation is crucial for forensic examinations, criminal investigations, and public health assessments. Delays could have serious consequences.

Legislation History and the Need for Action

This legislation was unanimously supported by the Health and Human Services Committee

in the 131st Maine Legislature, but it ultimately died in the Special Appropriations Table,
due to budget constraints. We ask this committee to once again approve this legislation

with LD 562 and ensure that it receives the necessary fundingthis session.

,

The Maine Funeral Directors Association strongly supports LD 562 because it provides a fair, necessary, and long-overdue adjustment to reimbursement rates. Maine's funeral practitioners are committed to supporting the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, law enforcement, and most importantly, Maine families in their most difficult moments. However, they cannot continue to absorb these costs at a loss.
We respectfully askthe committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 562 to ensure funeral
practitioners are fairly reimbursed for their essential services.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
Adam Walker President, Maine Funeral Directors Association

Adam Walker
President and Funeral Director

Testimony in Support of LD 562
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and Members of the Health and Human Services
Committee,

My name is Erik Tiner, and I am a fiineral service practitioner here in the great State of Maine. I
am a member of the Maine Funeral Directors Association (MFDA) Legislative Committee and
serve as Secretary on the Executive Board. The MFDA represents funeral practitioners from across the state. In addition, I manage Jones, Rich & Barnes and Lindquist Funeral Homes,
which serve Cumberland County.

I am here today to express my strong support for LD 562 as currently written.
First, I want to acknowledge that Maine's funeral service practitioners and the Office of the
Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) have enjoyed a long and productive professional relationship. Since the inception of the OCME, funeral service practitioners have been providing
transportation and removal services for human remains to the OCME in Augusta. This system has worked relatively well, with funeral service practitioners being contacted by the OCME to
transport human remains from the place of death and assist law enforcement officers as needed.

In many cases, the funeral service practitioners who are called to assist are local and may even
`
know the family of the deceased. This relationship allows us to offer a more personal and supportive service during an incredibly difficult time. However, an increasing number of cases
involve individuals with no family to claim them or those from outside the local area. In such instances, funeral service practitioners will shelter the remains at their facilities until a Deputy Medical Examiner can complete their examination and any necessary tests.
In 2011, this committee heard from us about the fact that our reimbursement from the OCME
had not increased since 1998. We were successful in advocating for a fee increase at that time, which was supported by the OCME. However, since then, costs have continued to rise, and
funeral service practitioners have been left behind in many OCME budget considerations. The
realities of inflation and rising operational costs are impacting funeral homes in Maine.
Some key factors to consider include: "

o The cost of a removal vehicle in 2011 was $24,000, but today it exceeds $35,000. o Licensing fees for funeral practitioners, funeral service establishments, and funeral

attendants have all risen since 2011, as have the costs of training requirements for these

I

licenses.

_

o Costs for labor, fuel, insurance, and the goods required to support OCME services have

all increased substantially.

It should be clear to all that Maine's funeral service practitioners can no longer be expected to
provide critical services to the OCME at a loss. Like any business, we must ensure that our costs
are covered. The reimbursement fees must be sufficient to meet the expenses incurred by funeral
practitioners when supporting the OCME.
Funeral practitioners across the state hope that the Health and Human Services Committee can fully appreciate the dilemma we face. It is not that we are unwilling to continue offering support to the OCME, but the simple fact is that we cannot afford to do so at a financial loss. If funeral
service practitioners are unable to continue providing these essential services, the burden will not
fall only on the OCME----it will directly affect the families who rely on the OCME's services and
the citizens of Maine at large.
Thank you for your consideration. We respectfully ask for your support in increasing
transportation fees for funeral service practitioners who assist the Office of the Chief Medical
Examiner.
Respectfully, Erik Tiner

Testimony in Support of LD 562 An Act to Update Reimbursement Rates for Transportation of Deceased Persons by Funeral
Homes When the Transport is at the Request of the Chief Medical Examiner

March 25, 2025

Senator Ingwersen, Rep. Meyer and Members of the Health and Human Services Committee. My name is Joseph Kiley, I live in Holden and own and operate Kiley & Foley Funeral Service in Bangor and Brewer
and my business serves the greater Bangor/Brewer community. I have been a licensed funeral practitioner since the early 90's and I am here today on behalf of the Maine Funeral Directors Association (MFDA) in support of LD 562
The State of Maine and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) in Augusta developed a
system in the 1980s for investigating deaths that fall under their jurisdiction. This system is a cooperative
where funeral homes transport human remains from the place of death to Augusta for required exams and are reimbursed for transportation costs. Since then, local funeral homes/practitioners have become the
point of contact for families that have experienced a death involving the OCME and the funeral home
becomes a facilitator/intermediary with the OCME, local law enforcement and the decedent's families.
This long standing relationship and understanding of each other's role and this process is generally smooth and trouble free.
Transportation reimbursement rates have not been adjusted since 2011 and prior to that since 1998.
Some of the typical factors that have driven cost upward for providing this transport service is vehicle cost
and maintenance, fuel, insurance, labor, licensing and training costs.
This bill was brought before this committee in the 131$` Legislature and was voted unanimously OTP out
of committee. It ultimately did not survive through appropriations so we bring this important bill to you
again. Since last year, as you may know, there have been some positive developments with the OCME.
There is a new facility being built to accommodate a greater need for forensic service and more advanced
testing. We also have a new Chief Medical Examiner, Dr. Alice Briones, who is from Maine, has some
impressive credentials having served as the head of the medical examiner system for the Dept of Defense and she and her staff are putting great emphasis on maintaining forensic accreditation, doing more
scientific identification when necessitated and emergency preparedness. With this being said, our
association and, I believe, the funeral practitioners around the state, are proud of the continued working relationship with the medical examiner's office that has been developed over a long period of time.
Funeral practitioners across the state are hopeful that this committee understands the need to address these
rates so that funeral homes are not continuing to absorb these costs. Without an increase in rates, we may
begin to lose some cooperation with these transport services that will ultimately affect its efficiency and
Maine families. We thank you for your consideration as we ask for your support for this increase that
support the medical examiner system. I would be happy to answer any questions about this process or any
related specifics.
Sincerely,
Joseph Kiley

RE: LD562: An Act to Update Reimbursement Rates for Transportation of Deceased Persons by Funeral Homes When the Transport is at the Request of the Chief Medical Examiner
Hello. I am Lindsey Chasteen, Office Administrator for the Maine Office of Chief Medical Examiner (OCME). I have worked at the OCME for almost 10 years and am testifying neither for nor against this bill.
The OCME is statutorily responsible (Title 22, Chap. 711) for determining the cause and manner of death of Maine's decedents that fall under our jurisdiction. The office has been accredited by the National Association of Medical Examiners (NAME) since 2017. Part of accreditation is conducting full, forensic autopsies when there is not an obvious cause of death. Maine's large geographical area prevents the OCME from responding to many of the death scenes, so transportation to Augusta, for autopsy, is provided by a local funeral home.
The reimbursement rates for funeral homes that transport at the request of the Office of Chief Medical Examiner are set within the OCME statute. The funding for this reimbursement comes from the OCME budget. In calendar year 2024 the OCME spent $98,051.00 in transportation expenses to funeral homes that conducted 991 transports to and from the OCME. I have included a chart comparing the current reimbursement rates to the proposed rates, and what expenses could look like on the next page.
Please note, the OCME cannot continue to operate at the current levels without the additional funding if this bill is passed. We require a fiscal note of $49,025.50 to adhere to the proposed change in reimbursement rates.
